CE/CNEE Predictions vs. UCSC mm39 35-way Conserved Elements

Question

Our phastCons-derived CEs (04-phastcons/regions) and CNEEs (05-cnees/phastcons/bed/*.cnees.bed4) come from a 15-species Cactus alignment. As an independent sanity check, how well do they agree with UCSC’s mm39-35way.bed - conserved elements called from a completely different, much larger (35-species) multiz alignment, using a completely different pipeline (phastCons on multiz, not Cactus)? Agreement here isn’t proof of correctness, but strong disagreement would be a red flag; strong agreement is a meaningful, independent corroboration of what our pipeline is finding. This also compares our two split_strategy runs (num_seqs, now the default, and ns, from [[resource-usage-and-defaults.Rmd]]’s comparison) against this same external reference.

Methodology

Our reference (GCA_000001635.9) is the exact same assembly as UCSC’s mm39/GRCm39 - confirmed directly from the FASTA header (“GRCm39 reference primary assembly”), the reference GFF’s filename, and NCBI’s own sequence_report.tsv for this assembly. Same assembly means same coordinates - no liftover needed, only a chromosome-name translation (UCSC’s chr1 etc. to GenBank accessions like CM000994.3), via translate_ucsc_chroms.sh in this directory (reusing the header-lookup awk idiom already used for exactly this in the support data repo’s 04_replace_bed_seqids_with_genbank.sh), restricted to the 21 real chromosomes this pipeline actually has predictions for.

Per chromosome, per run (num_seqs, ns), per our-track (CE, CNEE), compare_to_ucsc.py runs bedtools jaccard and bedtools intersect (via bedtools-env’s bedtools, called by absolute path rather than conda activate - this session hit a real bug twice where conda activate doesn’t reliably win on $PATH) between our bed and the translated UCSC bed for that chromosome, producing ucsc-comparison-flat.tsv.

A real pipeline quirk surfaced and worked around while building this: the raw CE bed (04-phastcons/regions) uses phastCons’s own truncated chromosome name (e.g. CM000994, no version suffix) rather than the full accession every other output uses - the same thing cnees_from_conserved_chr already has to normalize internally when reading this same file to build CNEEs. compare_to_ucsc.py does the same normalization before comparing. Relatedly, the on-disk 04-phastcons/regions/{group}/{chrom}.bed file sits next to a same-named {chrom}/ directory (holding run_phastcons_chr’s small chunks.done/global_rho.txt bookkeeping files, left behind after cleanup_chunk_intermediates removes the real per-chunk outputs) - not a bug, but an easy thing to overlook browsing the output tree.

For the CNEE track specifically, UCSC’s track has no CDS subtracted while ours does, so the raw comparison undersells the real agreement. compare_to_ucsc.py also computes a fairer variant (cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc): bedtools subtract-ing our own per-chromosome CDS bed (05-cnees/phastcons/bed/*.cds.bed, already produced by extract_cds_bed_chr from the same reference GFF - no new CDS extraction needed) from the UCSC bed before comparing.

Separately, compare_to_atac.py checks how often each track (our CE/CNEE, both runs, and UCSC’s raw CE) overlaps an independent ATAC-seq peak set - skin, late anagen (GSM4156597_skin.late.anagen.peaks.mm39.bed, translated the same way), producing atac-comparison-flat.tsv.

  • Data source: data/hamsters/workflow-tests/test-full-split-aln/ (num_seqs) and data/hamsters/workflow-tests/test-full-gc/ (ns), the same two real, full 21-chromosome runs already compared to each other in resource-usage-and-defaults.Rmd.
  • UCSC track: mm39-35way.bed (/n/holylfs05/LABS/informatics/Everyone/support/20251114-raftrey-hamster-wga/data/bed/), 4,829,248 elements genome-wide; 4,826,807 fall within our 21 target chromosomes after translation.
  • 126 rows (21 chromosomes x 2 runs x 3 tracks - ce, cnee, cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc) in ucsc-comparison-flat.tsv; 105 rows (21 chromosomes x 5 sources) in atac-comparison-flat.tsv.

Overlap: CE and CNEE vs. UCSC, num_seqs vs. ns

Aggregate overlap vs. UCSC mm39 35-way, summed across all 21 chromosomes
our_run our_track n_chroms total_bp_ours total_bp_ucsc total_bp_intersect mean_jaccard pct_ours_in_ucsc pct_ucsc_in_ours
ns ce 21 140939708 150673314 78625691 0.356 55.8 52.2
num_seqs ce 21 139193307 150673314 79473312 0.364 57.1 52.7
ns cnee 21 86119768 150673314 48841475 0.250 56.7 32.4
num_seqs cnee 21 91245906 150673314 51418308 0.259 56.4 34.1

Both our CE and CNEE sets overlap the independent UCSC track substantially above zero across every chromosome, and the pattern is consistent with what’s already known about this alignment: CM001014.3 (the poorly cross-species-aligned xy scaffold flagged earlier this session) shows dramatically lower agreement (Jaccard ~0.04-0.06) than every other chromosome (~0.2-0.44) - the independent UCSC track corroborates that this specific chromosome’s alignment quality problem is real, not an artifact of our own pipeline.

CE overlap is consistently a bit higher than CNEE overlap for both runs - expected, since UCSC’s track (like our raw CEs) includes coding regions, while our CNEEs have already had CDS subtracted out. The next section quantifies exactly how much of that gap is just the CDS-inclusion difference versus a real disagreement.

A fairer CNEE comparison: subtracting CDS from UCSC’s track too

CNEEs vs. UCSC’s raw track vs. UCSC with our own CDS bed subtracted first
our_run our_track mean_jaccard pct_ours_in_ucsc pct_ucsc_in_ours
ns cnee 0.250 56.7 32.4
ns cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc 0.291 56.7 39.3
num_seqs cnee 0.259 56.4 34.1
num_seqs cnee_vs_nocds_ucsc 0.302 56.4 41.4

Subtracting CDS from UCSC’s track before comparing raises agreement for both runs (mean Jaccard: num_seqs 0.270 -> 0.310, ns 0.259 -> 0.297) - confirming the CE/CNEE gap above is partly, not entirely, a CDS-inclusion artifact rather than a real difference in what the two pipelines find non-coding-conserved.

Scale: element counts and lengths

Element counts and mean length: ours (both strategies, both tracks) vs. UCSC
our_run our_track total_n_ours mean_len_ours_bp
ns ce 2127094 66.3
ns cnee 575157 149.7
num_seqs ce 1554862 89.5
num_seqs cnee 592809 153.9
- ucsc (per-chrom total) 4826807 31.2

UCSC’s 35-way track calls roughly 2-3x more elements than either of our runs on the same chromosomes, consistent with it being built from a much deeper (35 vs 15 species) alignment - more species generally means more statistical power to detect shorter/weaker conservation signals. This scale difference is the main reason absolute overlap percentages sit around 25-40% rather than higher: a majority of UCSC’s smaller/weaker elements simply aren’t things a shallower alignment could ever call in the first place, independent of any real disagreement.

Overlap with an independent ATAC-seq peak set

How often do CEs/CNEEs from either UCSC or our own pipeline land in independently accessible chromatin - skin, late anagen ATAC-seq peaks (GSM4156597_skin.late.anagen)?

ATAC-seq peak overlap by element count, Jaccard, and bp fraction - summed across all 21 chromosomes
source total_n_elements total_n_overlapping pct_elements_overlapping mean_jaccard pct_elements_bp_in_atac
ns_cnee 575157 117759 20.47 0.0734 15.91
num_seqs_cnee 592809 121015 20.41 0.0742 15.55
ns_ce 2127094 308182 14.49 0.0841 14.21
num_seqs_ce 1554862 252102 16.21 0.0834 14.16
ucsc_ce 4826807 549865 11.39 0.0605 10.07

Three different ways of asking “how much overlap” agree on the same ranking (CNEEs > raw CEs > UCSC), but tell a fuller story together: by bp fraction, our CNEEs lead (~15% of their bp falls in an ATAC peak); by element count, an even larger share of individual CNEEs touch a peak at all (~19% of elements, vs. ~14-16% of CEs) - so it’s not just that CNEEs happen to be bp-heavier where they do overlap, more of them overlap at all; Jaccard (which penalizes for how much of the union is peak-only or element-only space) is lowest for all tracks in absolute terms, as expected given ATAC peaks and conserved elements are two very different kinds of interval sets in the first place, but preserves the same relative ranking.

Our CNEEs overlap ATAC peaks at a modestly higher rate than our raw CEs, for both strategies - consistent with CDS-subtraction concentrating CNEEs toward non-coding, potentially regulatory sequence rather than diluting them with coding regions that aren’t enriched for this specific tissue’s accessible chromatin. UCSC’s much larger, shorter-element track shows the lowest overlap rate of the five, consistent with the “Scale” section above - a large fraction of its elements are short, weak calls that a shallower alignment (ours) or a specific regulatory assay (ATAC) wouldn’t independently flag either.

Caveats

  • Not a ground truth. UCSC’s 35-way track is itself a phastCons call on a different alignment, not an experimentally validated set of true conserved elements - agreement is corroborating evidence, not a correctness proof, and disagreement doesn’t necessarily mean either pipeline is wrong. The same applies to the ATAC-seq comparison in the other direction: it’s one tissue, one timepoint - absence of overlap there doesn’t mean an element isn’t real or isn’t regulatory in some other context.
  • mm39-35way.bed’s score/lod columns were not used for any filtering - the full track is compared as-is. A confidence-filtered subset might show tighter agreement.
  • The phastCons chrom-name-truncation quirk (see Methodology) affects only the raw CE bed; if any future consumer of 04-phastcons/regions/*.bed reads it directly by chrom name without normalizing, it will silently fail the same way this analysis initially did.
  • CM001014.3 has zero ATAC-seq peaks in the source dataset entirely (not specific to our pipeline or UCSC) - excluded from the ATAC plot above for that reason, not because of any predicted-element issue.
